title: Highest malignant potential colon polyp: villous adenoma
vignette: A 50-year-old woman comes to the office for a preventive examination. She feels well and has no ongoing symptoms. Medical and family histories are unremarkable. The patient does not use tobacco or alcohol. Blood pressure is 132/76 mm Hg and pulse is 72/min. BMI is 25 kg/m2. Physical examination is normal. The patient is up to date on breast and cervical screenings but has not undergone colon cancer screening. She is referred for colonoscopy, during which a single colon polyp is discovered. The polyp is removed and sent for microscopic examination. Which of the following pathologic findings would be associated with the greatest risk of malignant transformation?

clues.text: a single colon polyp is discovered
clues.note: Colon polyps are classified as neoplastic (adenomatous/sessile serrated - malignant potential) or non-neoplastic (hyperplastic, inflammatory, hamartomatous - generally benign).
Among adenomas, larger size, villous histology, and high-grade dysplasia carry the greatest cancer risk.

whatMatters: Neoplastic adenomas can transform into adenocarcinoma; risk rises with SIZE, VILLOUS histology, and high-grade dysplasia. Of the choices, a 2-cm VILLOUS ADENOMATOUS polyp has the greatest malignant potential (villous > tubulovillous > tubular; larger = worse). Answer D. (Hyperplastic, lymphoid, and hamartomatous polyps are generally benign.)
strategy: Rank by neoplastic potential: adenomatous (and sessile serrated) polyps are premalignant; among them, VILLOUS histology and LARGER size are the strongest risk factors. Pick the 2-cm villous adenoma. Reject the 2-cm tubular adenoma (lower risk than villous), and the non-neoplastic polyps: hyperplastic, sessile lymphoid, and hamartomatous (solitary sporadic hamartomas have essentially no malignant risk).

eliminations.label: Hyperplastic polyp - non-neoplastic (low risk)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: the most common non-neoplastic polyp - small, nondysplastic epithelial crypts. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: typical (small, left-sided) hyperplastic polyps have minimal malignant potential. ✅ Correct if: a benign incidental rectosigmoid polyp.

eliminations.label: Sessile lymphoid polyp - benign lymphoid tissue
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: benign, reactive lymphoid follicles bulging into the mucosa (often post-infectious). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it is non-neoplastic with essentially no malignant risk. ✅ Correct if: a benign lymphoid aggregate on colonoscopy.

eliminations.label: Tubular adenoma - neoplastic but lower risk than villous
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: an adenomatous (neoplastic) polyp with tubular architecture. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: tubular adenomas ARE premalignant but carry LOWER risk than villous adenomas of the same size. ✅ Correct if: comparing to a non-neoplastic polyp (tubular adenoma has higher risk than those).

eliminations.label: Hamartomatous polyp - non-neoplastic (solitary)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: disorganized native tissue (e.g., juvenile polyp). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: solitary sporadic hamartomatous polyps have essentially no malignant potential (risk rises only in hamartomatous polyposis SYNDROMES). ✅ Correct if: multiple polyps in a polyposis syndrome.

reasoning: Colon polyps split into neoplastic (adenomatous/sessile serrated) and non-neoplastic (hyperplastic, lymphoid, hamartomatous)
Only adenomatous polyps have significant malignant potential
Among adenomas, VILLOUS histology and larger SIZE confer the highest risk
mechanism: Colonic polyps are mucosal protrusions classified as NEOPLASTIC (adenomatous - tubular, tubulovillous, villous - and sessile serrated) or NON-NEOPLASTIC (hyperplastic, inflammatory, lymphoid, hamartomatous). Only NEOPLASTIC polyps carry meaningful potential to progress to colonic ADENOCARCINOMA (the adenoma-carcinoma sequence). Among adenomas, the risk of malignant transformation increases with (1) larger SIZE (the single most important factor - >1-2 cm is higher risk), (2) VILLOUS histology (villous > tubulovillous > tubular), and (3) higher-grade DYSPLASIA. Therefore a 2-cm VILLOUS adenoma has greater malignant potential than a 2-cm tubular adenoma, and far greater than the non-neoplastic options. Hyperplastic polyps (small, left-sided) are usually benign; sessile lymphoid polyps are benign reactive lymphoid tissue; and SOLITARY hamartomatous polyps (juvenile polyps) have essentially no malignant risk (though hamartomatous polyposis SYNDROMES do). This is why screening colonoscopy removes adenomatous polyps to prevent cancer.

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid GI > colon polyps: neoplastic (adenomatous/sessile serrated = malignant potential) vs non-neoplastic (hyperplastic, hamartomatous, inflammatory); risk factors = size, villous histology, high-grade dysplasia.

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: Villous histology + larger size = greatest malignant potential among adenomas.

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on adenomatous vs hyperplastic vs hamartomatous polyps, villous vs tubular, dysplasia, or adenoma-carcinoma sequence? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: Tubular adenoma is neoplastic but lower risk than villous; hyperplastic/lymphoid/hamartomatous (solitary) are non-neoplastic.

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: villous adenoma = highest malignant potential; risk rises with size, villous histology, high-grade dysplasia.

keywords.front: Colon polyp with greatest malignant potential

keywords.back: Neoplastic: adenomatous, sessile serrated; non-neoplastic: hyperplastic, hamartomatous, inflammatory
Essentially none (risk only in polyposis syndromes)

firstAid.detail: GI: villous adenoma highest malignant potential; size + villous + dysplasia.
GI > remove adenomas to interrupt adenoma-carcinoma sequence.

memoryHook: Villous = villainous: big villous adenomas are the polyps most likely to turn into cancer; hyperplastic and (solitary) hamartomatous polyps are bystanders.
